title: Saved by Mercy, Devoted to Good Works
summary: Paul tells Titus to remind the believers on Crete to be good citizens and gentle neighbors, because they themselves were once enslaved to their desires until God's kindness appeared and saved them by mercy, through the washing of new birth and the renewal of the Holy Spirit. Titus is to insist on good works, avoid pointless disputes, and warn divisive people twice before having nothing more to do with them. The letter closes with travel plans and greetings.
story: Titus is one of three letters, with 1 and 2 Timothy, addressed to Paul's co-workers and known together as the Pastoral Letters. Paul had left Titus on the island of Crete to set the young churches in order and appoint elders (Titus 1:5). Chapter 1 dealt with leaders and false teachers, and chapter 2 with how older and younger men and women and slaves should live so that the teaching about God would be honored. Chapter 3 widens the view to the church's life in public, before rulers and unbelieving neighbors, and grounds everything in one of the richest summaries of salvation in Paul's letters (verses 4-7). Then the letter ends as real letters do, with names, plans, and a request to hurry.
historical:
Whether Paul wrote the Pastoral Letters is one of the main authorship debates in the New Testament. The traditional view, held by many scholars today, is that Paul wrote them late in his life, after a release from the Roman imprisonment described at the end of Acts, in the early to mid 60s AD. Many other scholars hold that a follower of Paul wrote them in his name some decades later, pointing to differences of vocabulary, style, and church order from the undisputed letters. A middle view suggests Paul used a secretary who was given considerable freedom. Acts records Paul's ship stopping briefly at Crete on the way to Rome (Acts 27:7-13), but not a mission there, so the setting of Titus assumes events Acts does not narrate.

The names in verses 12-13 anchor the letter in Paul's circle. Tychicus appears in Acts 20:4 and carried Paul's letters to Ephesus and Colossae (Ephesians 6:21, Colossians 4:7). Apollos was the gifted teacher from Alexandria who worked in Ephesus and Corinth (Acts 18:24-28, 1 Corinthians 3:6). Artemas and Zenas are known only here. Several towns were named Nicopolis, meaning city of victory; most scholars think Paul meant the one in Epirus on the western coast of Greece, founded by Augustus to commemorate his victory at Actium in 31 BC.
cultural:
Crete was part of a combined Roman province with Cyrenaica in North Africa, and the letter's first chapter repeats a proverb about the islanders' bad reputation (Titus 1:12). The instructions to submit to rulers, be peaceable, and show consideration to everyone would have mattered for small, suspicious-looking groups that met privately and refused the gods of their neighbors. A reputation for good conduct protected the church and commended its message.

Verse 4 uses language a Greek reader associated with rulers. Philanthropia, love for humanity, was a virtue praised in kings and benefactors, and the verb for appear was used of a god's manifestation or a ruler's arrival. Paul applies these words to God's saving act in Christ: the true benefactor has appeared. Zenas is called a nomikos, a lawyer, which could mean an expert in Jewish law or a jurist in Roman law; the text does not say which. Travelers in the ancient world depended on churches and friends to supply them for the next stage of the road, and verse 13 asks Titus to do exactly that for Zenas and Apollos.
literary: The chapter has three movements. Verses 1-2 give public ethics. Verses 3-8 give the reason, set in a before-and-after pattern: "at one time we too were foolish" (verse 3), "But when the kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind appeared" (verse 4). Verses 4-7 are one long sentence in Greek, carefully balanced and possibly drawn from early Christian teaching or worship, and verse 8 calls it one of the trustworthy sayings, a formula that appears five times in the Pastoral Letters. Its structure is Trinitarian: God our Savior saved us, through the renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out through Jesus Christ our Savior. Verses 9-15 then return to practical matters, contrasting good works, which are "excellent and profitable", with controversies that are "pointless and worthless", before ending in travel plans and greetings. Notice the frame: good works in verse 1, verse 8, and verse 14.

outline.t: God's kindness appeared: saved by mercy, renewed by the Spirit
A trustworthy saying that leads to good works
Avoid foolish controversies and warn the divisive
Travel plans, provision for workers, and greetings

doctrines.note: Verses 4-7 state salvation with unusual fullness. Its source is God's kindness and love; its basis is mercy, "not by the righteous deeds we had done"; its means are new birth and the Spirit's renewal; its result is justification by grace and the hope of eternal life. Good works follow as its fruit, not its cause (verses 8, 14).

The Holy Spirit renews believers and is poured out on them abundantly through Jesus Christ (verses 5-6), language that echoes Joel's promise and the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:17, 33). New life is God's work within a person, not a moral improvement project.

Many interpreters read "the washing of new birth" as a reference to baptism, while others see a picture of the Spirit's inner cleansing. Traditions differ on how the washing and the new birth relate (see the hard question below).

The church is to be known in public for gentleness and good works, not for quarrels. Verses 10-11 give a simple discipline for a person who keeps dividing the community: two warnings, then separation.

words.note: Palingenesia, new birth or regeneration, literally becoming again. The only other New Testament use is Matthew 19:28, where it names the renewal of the whole world at the end of the age. Stoic philosophers used it for the rebirth of the cosmos, and Jewish writers used it for Israel's restoration. Here the renewal God will bring to all things has already begun in the believer.

Loutron, washing or bath. Its only other New Testament use is Ephesians 5:26, the washing with water through the word. Whether it refers directly to baptism or to the cleansing that baptism signifies is debated, but the washing in view is God's act, not ours.

Philanthropia, love for humankind, the root of the English word philanthropy. In Greek culture it was a virtue of kings and benefactors toward their subjects. Paul uses it of God himself, whose generosity toward human beings appeared in Christ (verse 4).

Hairetikos, divisive or factious, used only here in the New Testament. It later gave us the word heretic, but here it describes behavior more than doctrine: a person who forms factions and stirs up quarrels. Paul prescribes patience first (two warnings) and then refusal (verse 10).

christ: This chapter says plainly what Christ has done and why it matters for ordinary life. God's kindness and love "appeared" in the coming of Jesus, and salvation rests on God's mercy, not on anything the believer contributed. The same title, Savior, is given to God in verse 4 and to Jesus Christ in verse 6, and the chapter describes Father, Spirit, and Son acting together in one work of rescue, the pattern the church later confessed as the Trinity. Through Jesus the Spirit is poured out, and through his grace believers are justified and made heirs. The ethics of verses 1-2 follow from this: people who were rescued while they were "hated and hating one another" (verse 3) are to be gentle with the unbelievers they once resembled.

hard.q: Does "the washing of new birth" mean that baptism saves?
hard.a:
Christians read verse 5 in several ways. Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, and Lutheran traditions generally hold that it refers to baptism and that God truly gives new birth through baptism as his appointed means, though grace and faith remain essential and God is not bound by the rite. Reformed and Presbyterian traditions often read it as baptism understood as a sign and seal of the regeneration the Spirit works, connected to the reality but not automatically conveying it. Baptist and many other evangelical interpreters argue that the washing is the Spirit's inward cleansing, described with water imagery (as in Ezekiel 36:25-27), and that baptism is the public sign of what has already happened.

All of these readings agree on what the verse most plainly insists: salvation comes "not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy", and it is the Holy Spirit who renews. How baptism relates to that renewal is a real and longstanding second-order difference among faithful churches.

questions: Paul grounds gentleness toward outsiders in the memory of what believers once were (verse 3). How does remembering your own past change the way you treat people you disagree with?
Verses 4-7 describe salvation as entirely God's mercy, yet verses 8 and 14 insist on good works. How do these two emphases fit together?
What is the difference between a controversy worth having and one that is pointless and worthless (verse 9)?
